question.problem:
Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t\} & =\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>0, \\ L\{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t\} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

find $L\{u(t-5)\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\pi t)\},$ where $u(t)$ is the unit step function.
question.worked_solution:
The second shifting theorem states that if $a\ge 0$ and $L\{u(t-a)\,g(t)\}$ exists for $s>{s}_{0},$ then

$$
L\{u(t-a)\,g(t)\}={e}^{-as}\,L\{g(t+a)\},\,\text{for}\,s>{s}_{0},
$$

where $u(t)$ is the unit step function.

In our case, we wish to find

$$
L\{u(t-5)\,\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\pi t)\}.
$$

Therefore, $a=5,$ and we have 

$$
L\{u(t-5)\,g(t)\}={e}^{-5s}\,L\{g(t+5)\},
$$

where $g(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\pi t).$

Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}g(t+5) & =cos\,(5\pi (t+5)) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\pi t+25\pi ) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡5\pi t\operatorname{cos}⁡25\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡5\pi t\operatorname{sin}⁡25\pi  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡5\pi t\cdot (-1)-\operatorname{sin}⁡5\pi t\cdot 0 \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡5\pi t.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $L\{\operatorname{cos}⁡(\omega t)\}=\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}$ for $s>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{g(t+5)\} & =L\{-\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\pi t)\} \\  & =-L\{\operatorname{cos}⁡(5\pi t)\} \\  & =-\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+25{\pi }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the second shifting theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L\{u(t-5)\,g(t)\} & ={e}^{-5s}\,L\{g(t+5)\} \\  & =-{e}^{-5s}\cdot \frac{s}{{s}^{2}+25{\pi }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$
